packs.title: City Frames
packs.promise: Read Tokyo through station brickwork, a bay route and western city views.

q.s: Turn a tower’s repeated triangles into a small pattern.
st: Choose a comfortable public park-path position where the orange-and-white Tokyo Tower can be seen. Remain on the path.
Draw or describe one repeated lattice shape. Repeat it three times to make your own small pattern, then change the spacing of the last repeat.
Add a note about what your change does to the pattern. This is a drawing exercise; no tower climb, exact structural measurement or engineering claim is needed.

q.s: Build a usable rail plan before looking across the water.
st: Using the current Yurikamome route information, plan a journey from Shimbashi to Daiba. Record the direction, destination station and the current fare shown by the operator.
Add waiting time and the walk from Daiba to an open park boardwalk. The linked chart gives about fifteen minutes aboard the train; check current service before travelling.

If you take the journey, stop safely on the open boardwalk and describe one broad shape in the Rainbow Bridge view. If you stay where you are, use the official park image for that observation. Save the route plan and view note together.

q.s: Make a three-beat record of one park view.
st: Choose a comfortable open path position with a view of the pond, lawn or surrounding trees. Keep the water edge and through routes clear.
At the start, after roughly thirty seconds and after roughly a minute, add one small mark or word for a visible change. Moving light, a ripple or a leaf counts; listening is optional.
Place the three marks in sequence and give the sequence a short title of your own. If nothing changes visibly, record three details you notice in turn.

packs.title: Roofs and River
packs.promise: Find small patterns between Asakusa’s streets and the Sumida River.

q.s: Build a collection that leaves every object where it belongs.
st: Stand aside in Nakamise-dori, the shopping approach to Senso-ji, without occupying a shop entrance.
Collect three visible material impressions: something woven, something rigid, and something that catches light. Packaging, shutters and building details count; do not handle merchandise.
Describe each in two words, then arrange the six words into the order you would use for an imaginary pocket-sized street collage.

q.s: Reduce a big view to three deliberate strokes.
st: Find a safe riverfront viewpoint facing Tokyo Skytree across the Sumida River. You do not need to travel to or enter the tower.
Draw or describe the skyline with only three strokes: one for the river edge, one for the building mass, and one for the tower.
Add one sentence about which detail you chose to leave out. Your edit matters more than drawing skill.

q.s: Let a short crossing change one familiar view.
st: Start at the Asakusa end of the red Azuma-bashi bridge and choose a visible feature across the river.
If comfortable and the pedestrian route is open, cross at your own pace without stopping in narrow areas. Otherwise compare the near bank and far bank from one safe stationary view.
At a clear resting point, record one shape that stayed recognizable and one alignment that changed. The stationary comparison earns identical credit.
